# Co-constructing adaptive lesson plans with GenAI: Pre-service teachers’ Intelligent-TPACK and prompt engineering strategies

## ARTICLE INFO ABSTRACT

### _Keywords:_ Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) technologies present new opportunities for teachers to 

### Adaptive learning design adaptive and student-centered instruction. However, the educational value of GenAI de- Teacher education pends not only on technical usage but also on teachers’ ability to formulate pedagogically Intelligent-TPACK meaningful prompts. Prompting strategies are not isolated from teachers′ prior knowledge and 

Prompt engineering

### skills. Less is known about how pre-service teachers′ AI-related knowledge influences prompt 

engineering strategies, in turn leading to meaningful adaptive lesson plans. Considering this gap, we design an instructional task for pre-service teachers to generate adaptive lesson plans with the help of GenAI. Prior to the task, we collected data about their AI-related skills, namely AI literacy and Intelligent-TPACK. The prompts were qualitatively analyzed based on the phases of the Knowledge Construction (KC) Framework. Then, we explored the pedagogical value of adaptive lesson plans through a rubric in terms of three indicators: student agency, adaptive strategies, and flexible tools. PLS-SEM analysis revealed that as long as pre-service teachers have AI-specific technological and pedagogical knowledge, they formulate higher phases of prompts based on the KC framework. Our analysis showed that prompts from higher phases generated more adaptive lesson plans in terms of student agency, adaptive strategies, and flexible tools. We also found an indirect effect of Intelligent-TPK on adaptive lesson plans. This study highlights that effective prompt engineering is a pedagogical act shaped by teachers’ knowledge, not merely a technical command. It also underscores the importance of embedding AI-specific pedagogical training in teacher education. By conceptualizing prompts as epistemic moves, we offer new insights into how teachers and GenAI can collaborate to produce responsive and inclusive 

learning experiences.

## 1. Introduction

The growing emphasis on adaptive learning in education highlights the critical role of teachers’ knowledge and skills in responding to diverse student needs (Wang, Christensen, et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2025). It is a complex instructional task for teachers to design and implement adaptive learning process ([Bernacki et al., 2021)](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement). This is because it traditionally requires high levels of pedagogical expertise, real-time decision-making, and the ability to offer personalized support ([Arthars et al., 2019;](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement) Shemshack et al., 2021). With

This is an open access article under the CC BY license ([http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ )](http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). the advent of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) technologies, it has become increasingly feasible for teachers to design more personalized and responsive learning experiences (Hsia et al., 2025). This is because GenAI tools can support differentiation, scaf- folding, and learner agency (Yang & Markauskaite, 2025). However, teachers have a responsible role in the ethical and pedagogical use of GenAI technologies in designing adaptive teaching practices (Celik, 2023; Henderson et al., 2025; Tagare et al., 2025). GenAI tools such as ChatGPT, CoPilot, and Google Gemini, which are now widely used by teachers and students, are considered intelligent systems ([Ariza et al., 2025;](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement) Guggemos, 2024; Hong et al., 2025). For teachers to effectively integrate these tools into their practice, it is essential not just to understand how to use but also how to interact with them meaningfully (Guggemos & Seufert, 2021; Wang et al., 2025). A key component of this interaction is prompt formulation, which serves as the foundation for successful GenAI-assisted teaching (Hsu, 2025). The quality of AI-generated outcomes is largely determined by the user’s ability to craft effective prompts ([Cain, 2024;](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement) Lee and Palmer, 2025). This has led to the emergence of prompt engineering, defined as the strategic design of precise and purposeful inputs to guide AI tools in producing relevant and valuable outputs (Knoth et al., 2024). Well-crafted prompts can significantly enhance GenAI’s ability to support instructional tasks such as lesson planning. However, there is still limited un- derstanding of how to optimize prompt use in educational contexts. To strengthen teacher and GenAI collaboration, further research is needed to explore prompt engineering and identify strategies that provide the most effective support for teachers’ professional work (Celik et al., 2022; Cress & Kimmerle, 2023; Park & Choo, 2025).

Moreover, there is limited understanding of how these strategies intersect with teacher professional knowledge to ethically inte- grate GenAI into education. Indeed, ethical GenAI integration requires the teacher’s knowledge not only for technical use of GenAI tools but also pedagogical reasoning and ethical considerations (Guggemos, 2024). In this regard, teacher education institutions must equip future teachers not only with AI literacy but also with pedagogical competencies specific to AI-integrated instruction (Celik et al., 2024; Cheah et al., 2025). Pre-service teachers need structured opportunities to practice prompt engineering and critically evaluate GenAI outputs (Laru et al., 2025). In this way, they can align such outputs with learning goals and student needs. To better understand and support pre-service teachers’ ethical and pedagogical use of GenAI, the use of theoretically validated frameworks can provide essential guidance in this process.

An updated framework of Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) (Mishra & Koehler, 2006), Intelligent-TPACK addresses teacher knowledge to ethically integrate GenAI technologies in their instructional process (Celik, 2023). Similarly, AI lit- eracy knowledge and skills are crucial for future teachers to recognize and use AI technologies in daily life and education. Integrating prompt engineering with these frameworks can offer a more comprehensive overview of what teachers need to design effective AI-enhanced learning experiences. However, there remains a lack of empirical studies to understand pre-service teachers′ role in AI-related knowledge and skills for prompting strategies (Park & Choo, 2025). In this study, the Knowledge Construction (KC) framework (Gunawardena et al., 1997) guided us to better understand pre-service teachers’ prompting strategies. Accordingly, this framework posits that knowledge is constructed through five interrelated phases, suggesting that deeper knowledge is constructed at higher phases (e.g., negotiation of meaning) compared to lower ones (e.g., sharing information). In line with the KC framework, we assumed that prompts at higher phases would yield more meaningful GenAI outcomes in terms of adaptive learning. The aim of the current study is to explore the ways in which pre-service teachers engage in prompt engineering to design adaptive learning experiences with the help of GenAI tools. By analyzing their prompting strategies through the lens of the KC framework, we aim to identify how the phases of prompts influence the quality of GenAI-generated lesson plans. We also examine how these strategies intersect with pre-service teachers’ Intelligent-TPACK and AI literacy skills, providing insight into the competencies required for the ethical and pedagogically sound use of GenAI in education. Ultimately, this study contributes to emerging research on GenAI- integrated pedagogy by offering empirical evidence on how prompting strategies shape the design of personalized, responsive, and student-centered learning environments.

| _2.1._ | _Teachers’_  | _role in adaptive learning_ |  |
|  | Adaptive learning is  | an  | instructional approach in which learning pathways are adjusted to align with learners’ needs, prior  |

knowledge, and interests (Xie et al., 2019). In other words, it occurs when instruction is tailored to students’ progress and charac- teristics ([Arthars et al., 2019)](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement). Such adjustment requires a flexible pedagogical design to transform students’ progress and charac- teristics into meaningful instructional decisions (Loughland & Alonzo, 2019). In the pedagogical designs for adaptive learning, the role of teachers is central. More specifically, teachers are expected to plan, implement, and assess instruction with attention to students’ diverse needs (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). To achieve this, they must balance subject matter knowledge with developmental, contextual, and ethical considerations (Celik, 2023; Shemshack et al., 2021).

For teachers to design a meaningful adaptive learning process, students are given some choices to select different learning activities (Holstein et al., 2020, pp. 1–15). This process is mainly related to student agency, which is a key aspect of adaptive lesson designs. For instance, students may decide the pace of their work, select resources that match their learning goals. In addition, teachers should also define their strategies to scaffold learners for achieving an adaptive learning task. Scaffolding strategies are important in designing adaptive learning environments as they provide timely support within structured guidance and help learners manage cognitive de- mands (Van de Pol et al., 2010). In an adaptive learning design, the planned use of technology is also a critical dimension. Technology provides learners with flexibility by enabling differentiated tasks, varied representations, and adjustable pacing (Xie et al., 2019). Teachers, however, are responsible for orchestrating this flexibility, ensuring that digital tools are aligned with learning goals and integrated in ways that support student agency and scaffolded progression (Wei et al., 2025).

In sum, teachers should consider student agency, scaffolding strategies, and technology use as flexible tools when designing adaptive learning environments. These three elements work together to ensure that learners are both supported and empowered, while instruction remains responsive to diverse needs. The current study addresses adaptive learning through these concepts by examining how lesson plans incorporate opportunities for student choice, the presence of scaffolding strategies, and the integration of flexible technological tools.

### _2.2._ _Intelligent-TPACK_

The Intelligent TPACK framework is a contemporary extension of the TPACK framework developed by Mishra and Koehler (2006). It was proposed in response to the growing integration of AI technologies into educational settings. This framework aims to define the specific professional knowledge for teachers to ethical and pedagogical use of AI-enhanced tools (Celik, 2023). [Fig. 1](#22-intelligent-tpack) shows TPACK and Intelligent-TPACK frameworks.

The Intelligent TPACK framework emphasizes the importance of teacher competencies not only in using AI tools pedagogically meaningful and ethically responsible. It has five AI specific following components: Technology Knowledge (Intelligent- TK), Intelligent Technological Content Knowledge (Intelligent-TCK), Intelligent Technological Pedagogical Knowledge (Intelligent -TPK), Intelligent Technological Pedagogical and Content Knowledge (Intelligent-TPACK).

_Intelligent-TK_, which refers to knowledge about how AI systems operate and how to use them effectively; _Intelligent-TPK_, which focuses on the pedagogical application of AI tools to support student-centered instruction, differentiation, and formative assessment; and _Intelligent-TCK_, which involves the use of AI tools to represent and explore subject-specific content. The integration of these do- mains results in Intelligent-TPACK, which represents a teacher’s ability to design, implement, and evaluate instructional activities that effectively combine AI technologies with appropriate pedagogical strategies and subject matter knowledge. Importantly, the frame- work addresses the need for critical AI literacy, including awareness of ethical concerns such as bias, transparency, data privacy, and the role of human judgment in AI-supported decision-making. Teachers are expected to engage in human-AI co-agency, where the teacher retains pedagogical control while leveraging AI tools to augment learning experiences.

Overall, the Intelligent TPACK framework provides a comprehensive model for preparing educators to navigate the complexities of AI-enhanced education by aligning AI capabilities with pedagogical goals and learners’ needs in ethically grounded ways (Celik, 2023).

### _2.3._ _AI literacy_

To navigate the increasing presence of AI-based technologies in society and education, individuals must possess a broad and in- tegrated set of knowledge, skills, and values that enable both effective use and ethical engagement (Ng et al., 2021). This necessity has given rise to the emerging concept of AI literacy, which reflects a shift in how technological competencies are understood in the 21st century (Long & Magerko, 2020). AI literacy is broadly defined as the capacity to interact with AI systems in a manner that is both informed and responsible, encompassing technical understanding and critical awareness (Long & Magerko, 2020). Historically, literacy was narrowly framed as the ability to read and write (Willinsky, 2017). However, technological advancement has transformed literacy into a multifaceted concept that extends far beyond traditional boundaries. Contemporary frameworks now 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 1.** TPACK ([tpack.org)](http://tpack.org) and Intelligent-TPACK (Celik, 2023) frameworks.

recognize various forms of new literacies, including media, information, digital, and AI literacies, which demand additional cognitive, ethical, and operational skills (Griffin & Care, 2014; Kong et al., 2021; Laru et al., 2025). Among these, AI literacy is increasingly seen as essential for full participation in a society shaped by intelligent systems.

Despite its importance, AI literacy remains an evolving construct with limited consensus around a comprehensive definition (Chiu et al., 2024). Nonetheless, prevailing views emphasize that AI literacy involves not only understanding how to operate AI tools but also recognizing their ethical implications, such as fairness, bias, transparency, and accountability (Steinbauer et al., 2021). This is especially pertinent because ethical decisions in AI development are often made by technical experts without sufficient attention to end-users’ perspectives, capacities, or values (Holmes et al., 2021). Hence, fostering ethical sensitivity among AI users is crucial for ensuring responsible use and promoting socially inclusive outcomes.

To provide conceptual clarity, Ng et al. (2021) conducted a systematic and exploratory review using Bloom’s taxonomy as an organizing framework. Their model defines AI literacy as comprising three progressive levels: knowledge and comprehension, application, and evaluation and development. This model emphasizes the integration of data science and computational thinking within a multidisciplinary framework, highlighting that ethical awareness, particularly regarding fairness and transparency in AI systems, is a fundamental component of AI literacy (Ng et al., 2021). Importantly, these skills are not only relevant for developers but are also essential for educators, students, and everyday users who interact with AI in personal and professional contexts (Long & Magerko, 2020). AI literacy also requires an awareness of AI’s limitations, such as its black-box nature, potential for biased outputs, and susceptibility to misinformation (Steinbauer et al., 2021). Thus, individuals must be equipped to critically interrogate AI-generated information and avoid overreliance on its outputs. As [Casal-Otero et al. (2023)](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement) argue, such competencies empower users to adopt a reflective and informed stance toward the expanding ecosystem of AI-driven tools, including large language models. To guide this study, we draw upon the AI literacy framework proposed by Wang et al. (2023), which defines AI literacy as the ability to recognize, use, evaluate, and ethically engage with AI technologies. This framework delineates four key dimensions: _Awareness_, which involves recognizing the presence and relevance of AI technologies and developing a conceptual understanding of how they function. It is viewed as a prerequisite cognitive process that underlies meaningful AI use (Wang et al., 2023). _Usage_, which refers to the practical and operational ability to utilize AI tools for various tasks. This includes technical fluency and interaction skills in educational and everyday contexts (Wang et al., 2023). _Evaluation_, which encompasses the critical capacity to assess the appropriateness, reli- ability, and biases of AI-generated outputs. Given the opaque and probabilistic nature of many AI systems, users must exercise discerning judgment when relying on these tools (Hermann, 2022). _Ethics_, which emphasizes the user’s responsibility in the use of AI. This includes understanding the societal impacts, risks, and normative expectations of AI integration, ensuring that such tools are used in ways that respect human dignity and democratic values (Wang et al., 2023).

Together, these dimensions form a holistic foundation for developing responsible and competent AI users. As AI technologies become increasingly embedded in education and daily life, advancing AI literacy among pre-service teachers and learners will be critical for fostering thoughtful, equitable, and effective human-AI collaboration.

### _2.4._ _Prompt engineering and knowledge construction_

Nowadays teachers incorporate GenAI tools into their teaching practices. In this process, the quality and relevance of AI-generated outputs depend on the structure and clarity of the teacher’s prompts (Knoth et al., 2024). In educational contexts, well-designed prompts can guide GenAI tools to deliver more focused, pedagogically aligned, and context-aware responses (Walter, 2024). This reflects the growing importance of prompt engineering, defined as the deliberate and strategic construction of prompts to optimize the utility of AI tools in producing meaningful educational outcomes ([Cain, 2024;](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement) Holmes et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2024). Prompt en- gineering thus plays a crucial role in shaping not only the relevance but also the pedagogical validity of AI outputs (Knoth et al., 2024). For teachers to use GenAI tools effectively, they must craft prompts that encourage the AI to engage substantively with instructional goals and deliver responses aligned with intended learning outcomes (Powell & Courchesne, 2024). When prompts are designed with pedagogical depth, GenAI tools can provide tailored suggestions for diverse teaching activities such as lesson planning, formative assessment, and technology integration (Lee and Palmer, 2025).

In this study, the KCF (Gunawardena et al., 1997) was utilized as the overarching framework for the analysis of pre-service teachers’ prompt engineering strategies. This approach diverges from the conventional application of extant typologies, including Input–Output Prompting (IOP) (Reynolds & McDonell, 2024), Chain-of-Thought (CoT) (Wei et al., 2022), and Tree-of-Thought (ToT) (Yao et al., 2023). The term IOP is used to denote simple, direct prompts that are designed to retrieve factual or procedural information from the AI. In IOP, the user inputs a question or command and expects a straightforward output without further elaboration or reasoning (Kojima et al., 2022; Reynolds & McDonell, 2024; Robertson, 2024). Meanwhile, CoT involves prompting AI to reason step-by-step before arriving at a final answer (Wei et al., 2022). ToT facilitates the exploration of multiple reasoning paths by the AI in a simultaneous manner, thereby expanding the capabilities of CoT. The AI explores multiple ideas or possible answers concurrently. The AI can then select the optimal idea by comparing the various options and disregarding the weaker ones (Yao et al., 2023). The selection of the KC framework was made on the basis of both theoretical alignment and research objectives. Accordingly, the KC framework emphasizes the cognitive depth and dialogic quality of knowledge construction. Since our objective was to understand how pre-service teachers engage with GenAI to design adaptive lesson plans, we needed a lens that captures not just the form of prompting (e.g., whether it includes stepwise reasoning or expert roles) but the underlying epistemic moves. Such moves appear as questioning, negotiating meaning, testing synthesis, or applying new knowledge. The KC framework thus allowed us to assess the pedagogical depth of prompts and their potential to co-construct instructional knowledge with GenAI (Cress & Kimmerle, 2023). While KC framework was originally designed to analyze human–human online interactions (Lucas et al., 2014), we adapted it to examine 

teacher–GenAI collaboration. We recognize that such interactions are not epistemically equivalent. In other words, unlike a peer, GenAI has no capacity to intentionally produce, justify, and take responsibility for knowledge claims, which is described as epistemic agency (Celik et al., 2025;Stroupe, 2014). However, functionally, GenAI responses can play a role similar to peer contributions by introducing new information, generating dissonance, and prompting negotiation of meaning ([An et al., 2025;](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement) Zhang & Wang, 2025). In this sense, although AI cannot be considered an epistemic equal, its outputs serve as dialogic triggers that scaffold pre-service teachers’ knowledge construction processes. Thus, the KC framework remains useful for capturing the human-driven but AI-supported cycles of refinement, testing, and integration of knowledge.

In this study, the “knowledge” constructed through prompting refers specifically to the co-construction of _instructional knowledge_ in the form of adaptive lesson plans. While pre-service teachers relied on their existing pedagogical and technological knowledge (e.g., Intelligent-TPACK, AI literacy), the KC framework was employed to examine how this knowledge was enacted and transformed through dialogic interaction with GenAI. Thus, the framework allowed us to move beyond viewing prompts as technical commands and instead conceptualize them as epistemic moves through which teachers and GenAI collaboratively shaped lesson design. The outcome of this process was not only the final lesson plan but also the iterative refinement of pedagogical reasoning. In their in- teractions with AI, teachers negotiated meaning, resolved dissonance, and tested synthesis.

The KC framework outlines five phases: (1) the sharing and comparison of information; (2) the discovery of dissonance; (3) the negotiation of meaning; (4) the testing and modification of proposed synthesis; and (5) the agreement and application (Gunawardena et al., 1997). These phases progress from surface-level exchange to deep cognitive engagement and knowledge co-construction. We focused on four phases of the KC framework, excluding the final phase. The rationale behind this is that the final phase requires the implementation of co-conducted knowledge (i.e. lesson plan) in a practical context.

Sharing and comparing information (Phase 1) involves participants introducing ideas, facts, or observations without attempting to reconcile differences. Discovery and exploration of dissonance (Phase 2) marks the point at which learners notice contradictions, gaps, or inadequacies in the information. Prompts in this phase may question the relevance or appropriateness of AI-generated responses (e. g., “This doesn’t seem age-appropriate. Is there a simpler way to explain it?”). Negotiation of meaning and co-construction of knowledge (Phase 3) entails efforts to resolve dissonance by integrating perspectives, elaborating ideas, or formulating interpretations. Here, users engage in deeper dialogic interaction with GenAI, refining the instructional design collaboratively (e.g., “Can you suggest ways to make this more engaging for visual learners?”). Testing and modification of proposed synthesis (Phase 4) focuses on evaluating the viability of constructed ideas and refining them through iterative feedback. Prompts aligned with this phase critically assess earlier responses, seeking improvements or alternatives (e.g., “Can you revise this activity to better support pupils with learning difficulties?”).

We argue that prompts negotiating the idea and testing in an iterative process can lead GenAI to generate more meaningful out- comes (Celik et al.,2022; Cress & Kimmerle, 2023). This is because such an iterative process gives an agency to pre-service teachers for checking and questioning the outcomes. It is worth noting that in this study, pre-service teachers’ knowledge is mainly constructed with a focus on adaptive lesson design. While GenAI provides suggestions, it does not construct knowledge independently; instead, it serves as a dialogic partner whose outputs are shaped by pre-service teachers’ prompts (Zhang & Wang, 2025). Through iterative prompts, teachers guide GenAI to produce outputs that better align with educational goals. In this way, pre-service teachers refine their instructional knowledge while steering GenAI toward more pedagogically meaningful contributions. The KC framework was therefore applied to capture this dialogic process, emphasizing how prompts function as epistemic moves that support the co-construction of adaptive lesson plans.

## 3. Present study

The integration of generative AI (GenAI) technologies into educational practice has introduced both significant opportunities and complex challenges for teacher education. While GenAI tools can support teachers in designing more adaptive and student-centered learning experiences, effectively leveraging these tools requires new forms of professional knowledge, including prompt engineering strategies, AI literacy, and ethical-technological reasoning (Celik, 2023; [Cain, 2024;](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement) Jari et al., 2025; Knoth et al., 2024). Despite increasing discourse on the potential of GenAI in pedagogy, empirical research remains limited on how pre-service teachers engage with these tools to generate instructional content that responds to learner diversity. This gap is especially evident in the context of adaptive lesson planning, where the quality of GenAI-generated outputs depends heavily on the design and intent of the prompts provided. To address this, the current study examines how pre-service teachers utilize GenAI tools to co-construct adaptive lessons and how these interactions with GenAI reflect their pedagogical reasoning and technological fluency.

To investigate this further, the first research objective (Obj1) focuses on uncovering how pre-service teachers formulate and refine prompts when designing adaptive lesson plans with GenAI support. This challenge involves not only technical formulation but also an understanding of how prompts elicit outputs that reflect differentiation, scaffolding, and student agency (Holstein et al., 2020, pp. 1–15; Walter, 2024; Zheng et al., 2024). However, it remains unclear what kinds of instructional elements emerge from these AI-generated lesson plans and how these elements reflect the cognitive depth of the user’s prompting strategies. To explore this, we applied the KC framework (Gunawardena et al., 1997) as an analytic lens for evaluating the phases and complexity of prompts. By aligning prompt strategies with distinct phases of KC, we aim to understand how higher-order prompts contribute to more meaningful GenAI-generated instructional outputs (Cress & Kimmerle, 2023; Garrison et al., 2003).

The second research objective (Obj2) addresses the individual knowledge factors that may shape pre-service teachers’ ability to engage in effective prompt engineering. Specifically, it investigates the extent to which participants’ AI literacy and Intelligent-TPACK levels are associated with the phases of their prompts, which then lead to the pedagogical quality of AI-generated lesson plans. Prior 

research suggests that these knowledge domains—technical, pedagogical, and ethical—are foundational for responsible and effective GenAI use in education (Celik et al., 2022; Ng et al., 2021). However, little is known about how these competencies interact with prompting behavior and influence GenAI outputs. By integrating AI literacy (Wang et al., 2022) and Intelligent-TPACK frameworks (Celik et al., 2022), this study seeks to uncover whether more knowledgeable pre-service teachers can more effectively utilize GenAI tools toward the generation of contextually adaptive and pedagogically sound learning experiences. To achieve these research ob- jectives, we defined the following research questions (RQs). 

- RQ1-Obj1: How do pre-service teachers employ prompt engineering strategies to generate adaptive lesson plans, and what instructional features emerge from these plans?
- RQ2-Obj2: What are the associations of pre-service teachers’ AI literacy and Intelligent-TPACK skills with their prompt engineering strategies and AI-generated adaptive lesson plans?

These research questions are tested through the research model illustrated below in [Fig. 2.](#4-methods)

## 4. Methods

### _4.1._ _Participants_

A total of 120 pre-service teachers were in the first phase of their five-year MA degree in a two-stage teacher education programme (Bachelor 3 years, Master 2 years) in Finland. Among these, 100 were enrolled in the classroom teacher education program and 20 were enrolled in the special education teacher education program.

### _4.2._ _Task: generation of adaptive lesson plan_

In order to investigate the ability of pre-service teachers to collaborate with GenAI tool for adaptive lesson planning, participants were asked to complete a structured task that simulated a real-life instructional scenario (see [Appendix A)](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement). They were asked to imagine that they were primary school teachers preparing a 45-min science lesson for a 5th-grade classroom consisting of 28 pupils (15 boys and 13 girls with an average age of 10). The learning objectives were to explain the stages of the water cycle (evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection) and to emphasize the importance of water in the environment. Participants were instructed to use a GenAI tool (Copilot) to generate teaching activities tailored to learning goals and pupil characteristics, to support their planning.

Crucially, the task emphasized designing adaptive or personalized instructional strategies by encouraging pre-service teachers to request support from the AI that considered pupil diversity, engagement, and differentiated learning needs. For this task, participants worked in pairs, resulting in 60 lesson plans being submitted in total. Each pair was given 15–20 min to interact with the AI and refine their instructional approach using iterative prompts. Afterwards, participants submitted a final AI-generated lesson plan justifying their choices. To better understand this justification, we also asked participants to reflect on the factors that influenced their decisions. At the end of the task, we collected the lesson plans, prompts, and their reflections.

**Fig. 2.** Tested research model.

### _4.3._ _Data collection tools_

#### _4.3.1._ _Intelligent-TPACK_

The Intelligent-TPACK Scale (Celik, 2023) was used to measure pre-service teachers’ professional knowledge for pedagogically and ethically integrating AI-based tools into instruction. The scale consists of 27 items distributed across five dimensions: Intelligent Intelligent-TK (5 items, α = .856), Intelligent-TPK (7 items, α = .858), Intelligent-TCK (4 items, α = .868), Intelligent TPACK (7 items, α = .895), and Ethics (4 items, α = .864). Each item was rated on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). All subscales demonstrated strong internal consistency, indicating the reliability of the scale for assessing AI-specific peda- gogical and ethical knowledge in teacher education contexts.

#### _4.3.2._ _AI literacy_

To evaluate participants’ understanding of, and ability to use, recognize and evaluate AI technologies, we used the AI Literacy Scale (AILS), which was developed by Wang, Rau and Yuan (2022). The scale is grounded in a four-factor model of AI literacy, encompassing awareness, usage, evaluation, and ethics. The final version of the AILS consists of 12 items (three per construct), which are rated on a 7- point Likert scale. Reliability scores for the subscales were satisfactory: awareness (α = .73), usage (α = .75), evaluation (α = .78), and ethics (α = .73). The overall scale demonstrated strong internal consistency (α = .83). Confirmatory factor analysis supported the four- factor structure, and model fit indices (e.g., CFI = 0.99, RMSEA = 0.01) confirmed the robustness of the theoretical model. This scale is a validated instrument for measuring individuals’ general AI literacy across cognitive, operational, evaluative, and ethical dimensions.

#### _4.3.3._ _Adaptive lesson plan rubric_

The final lesson plan selected by each pair of participants was evaluated using an adaptive lesson plan rubric. For this rubric and its dimensions, we used prior validated rubrics to technologically and pedagogically assess teachers′ instructional activities (Harris & Hofer, 2011; Koh, 2013; Kopcha et al., 2014). The rubric consists of three key dimensions: (1) adaptive strategies and scaffolding, (2) student agency, and (3) flexible content and tools. The first dimension focused on how the plan incorporated responsive instructional strategies and provided scaffolding for learning based on pupils’ varying needs. The second dimension addressed the level of student autonomy and opportunities for personalized learning pathways. The third dimension evaluated the flexibility and appropriateness of learning materials and tools for supporting differentiated instruction. This rubric enabled us to systematically assess the adaptive qualities embedded in the AI-generated content, as influenced by the pedagogical framing in pre-service teachers’ prompts Scoring of the lesson plans ranged from one to four (1: Limited, 2: Basic, 3: Proficient, 4: Excellent).

#### _4.3.4._ _Prompt engineering strategies_

To conceptualize the process of collaborative knowledge construction in pre-service teachers’ interactions with generative AI, we adopted the coding scheme developed by Gunawardena et al. (1997). This framework was originally designed for analyzing asyn- chronous online discussions and has since been widely applied and validated in both theoretical and empirical contexts (Lucas et al., 2014). 

1. Sharing and Comparing Information (KCP1): Participants ask basic questions or share factual information without integration.
2. Discovery and Exploration of Dissonance (KCP2): Prompting reflects identification of inconsistencies or gaps in understanding, often by questioning or challenging the initial ideas.
3. Negotiation of Meaning and Co-construction of Knowledge (KCP3): Prompts begin to synthesize ideas, suggesting hypotheses or integrating multiple perspectives.
4. Testing and Modification of Proposed Synthesis (KCP4): The user probes the AI’s responses more critically, refining their under- standing or seeking clarification based on the AI’s prior output.

The fifth phase of KC framework, “agreement and application,” was excluded because it requires the practical implementation of the collaboratively constructed knowledge in a real-world learning environment. Our task design asked pre-service teachers to generate and refine an adaptive lesson plan with GenAI support, but not to enact or evaluate this plan in classroom practice. Therefore, the final phase could not be meaningfully coded within the scope of this study. Focusing on the first four phases allowed us to capture the epistemic moves that occurred during the human–AI interaction itself, without extending beyond the boundaries of the task. [Fig. 3](#43-data-collection-tools) shows research design and its relevant stages.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 3.** Research design and its stages.

### _4.4._ _Data analysis_

To answer RQ1, two different coding approaches were applied. First, the Copilot outcome selected by pre-service teachers from Copilot was evaluated using the adaptive lesson plan rubric. Second, all prompts generated by pre-service teachers during the task were coded according to the KCP. Thus, while only the final Copilot output was analyzed with the rubric, each teacher prompt was classified based on the KC framework. To make sure the results of the coding were reliable, the first and second authors of the study randomly picked about 15 % of the lesson plan (_N_ = 4) and prompt engineering (_N_ = 4) data from the whole dataset and coded them separately (Fleiss et al., 2013). We calculated the Cohen’s Kappa score between the two coders as 0.65 for prompt engineering and 0.72 for the lesson plan. According to Landis and Koch (1977), values between 0.61 and 0.80 indicate substantial agreement in inter-rater reliability. Therefore, the coding consistency between the two raters was sufficiently strong to support further analyses. To examine the relationships among the research variables (RQ2), we applied partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) (Ringle & Sarstedt, 2016). This method is well suited for testing complex models and the interconnections between con- structs, which are operationalized through observed variables (Henseler et al., 2016). In addition, it places fewer restrictions on sample size. The PLS-SEM procedure follows two main stages. First, the measurement model is assessed to establish the reliability and validity of the constructs (Ringle & Sarstedt, 2016). Next, the structural model is analyzed to investigate the relationships among the constructs within the research model (Henseler et al., 2009).

The measurement model was built if convergent validity was ensured. To check this validity, three parameters were examined against established thresholds: (i) item reliability, evaluated through factor loadings (_\>_0.70), (ii) composite reliability for each construct (_\>_0.70), and (iii) average variance extracted (AVE _\>_0.50). Among these, the average value extracted is considered a particularly important criterion for convergent validity (Fornell & Larcker, 1981).

In the research model, the relationships were tested by estimating standardized regression weights (betas, _β_), including both direct and indirect effects among the constructs. Second, the structural model was examined by assessing path coefficients, their significance through 1000 bootstrapping, the coefficient of determination (R2), effect sizes (f2), and predictive relevance (Q2). The model’s approximate fit was further evaluated using the standardized root mean square residual (SRMR), which was below the recommended threshold of 0.08, indicating acceptable fit. The analyses were conducted using SmartPLS 4.

## 5. Results

### _5.1._ _The analysis of prompting strategies and lesson plans for adaptive learning (RQ1)_

After the task was completed, we collected 60 task files. Before qualitatively coding the prompts and lesson plans, we first identified how many prompts were used in each file. In the three task files, only one prompt was recorded. In five files, four prompts were used. In 32 files, we observed three prompts, and in 20 files, two prompts were generated. This distribution indicates the majority of pre-service teachers engaged with GenAI through two or three prompts when constructing their lesson plans \[1 prompt (_n_ = 3); 2 prompts (_n_ = 20); 3 prompts (_n_ = 32); 4 prompts (_n_ = 5)\].

[Fig. 4](#44-data-analysis) illustrates an example of how pre-service teachers’ prompts were classified into phases of the KC Framework (e.g., Phase 1, Phase 3, Phase 4) in the process of generation of adaptive lesson plan.

Each prompt generated an outcome, which the teacher pair evaluated and refined. This iterative process continued across multiple phases, with prompts functioning as epistemic moves that shaped successive outcomes. At the end of the task, participants selected an outcome namely the adaptive lesson plan. While each prompt was coded according to its KC phase, only the final outcome was assessed for pedagogical quality.

Furthermore, pre-service teachers′ prompting strategies based on the KC framework are presented in [Table 1.](#52-the-interplay-of-ai-literacy-intelligent-tpack-prompt-engineering-strategies-and-lesson-plans-for-adaptive-learning-rq2)

As shown in [Table 1,](#52-the-interplay-of-ai-literacy-intelligent-tpack-prompt-engineering-strategies-and-lesson-plans-for-adaptive-learning-rq2) most of the prompts (37.1 %) were related to KCP 3: Negotiation of Meaning. This suggests that pre-service teachers often engaged in pedagogical reasoning by asking GenAI to elaborate, justify, or refine instructional ideas. KCP 1: Sharing and comparing information was also frequent (32.1 %), which shows that they relied on basic descriptive prompts to generate lesson content. Prompts classified under KCP 2: Discovery and Exploration of Dissonance (15.7 %) showed that some pre-service teachers

The highest overall score was for adaptive strategies/scaffolding dimensions, indicating that pre-service teachers frequently incorporated moderate to high levels of instructional support into their lesson plans. For example, the lesson plans included group work and visual aids. Yet, there were some cases showing hands-on experimentation and teacher-guided station rotations. The student agency dimension indicates that, although many lesson plans included some level of pupils’ engagement and participation, only a few encouraged pupils to make autonomous choices or reflect on their learning. High-agency examples allowed pupils to select learning formats and presentation tools, demonstrating greater ownership of the learning process. The ’flexible content and tools’ dimension had a similar average, with most lesson designs using at least two content formats (for example, drawing and video) or different learning materials. The best plans let students use different types of media to show what they understand, while the more traditional plans only let students use the media that the teacher chooses.

The initial model included all paths from AI literacy and Intelligent-TPACK to prompting strategies and adaptive learning dimensions. After removing insignificant paths, the final model demonstrated acceptable fit, with an SRMR value of 0.043, below the recommended threshold of 

0.08 (Hair et al., 2022). The R2 values of the endogenous constructs ranged from 0.32 to 0.54, indicating moderate to substantial explanatory power. Predictive relevance (Q2) values were greater than zero for all endogenous variables, confirming the model’s predictive validity. [Fig. 5](#6-discussion) illustrates the final model.

The number of prompts was positively associated with Intelligent-TK (_β_ = 0.27) and Intelligent-TPK (_β_ = 0.26). Additionally, the number of prompts showed a positive relationship between participants’ awareness (_β_ = 0.23) and usage of AI (_β_ = 0.29). The phase of prompts was also significantly and positively associated with TK (_β_ = 0.30), TPK (_β_ = 0.32). Further, AI-related awareness (_β_ = 0.28) and usage (_β_ = 0.30) are related to the phase of prompts. Moreover, the number and phase of prompts were found to be interrelated (_β_ = 0.35).

Phase of prompts are associated with flexible tools (_β_ = 0.31), student agency (_β_ = 0.27), and adaptive strategies (_β_ = 0.25). Lastly, the PLS-SEM analysis yielded an indirect effect between TPK and both adaptive strategies (_β_ = 0.17; 95 % CI \[0.06, 0.29\]) and student agency (_β_ = 0.20; 95 % CI \[0.09, 0.33\]). This indirect effect was through the phase of prompts.

## 6. Discussion

The integration of GenAI into education has given rise to a number of critical questions concerning the knowledge and strategies that teachers will require in order to collaborate effectively with AI systems. While emerging literature highlights the technological and pedagogical potential of GenAI tools to support personalized learning, differentiation, and instructional design (Zhang et al., 2025), far less is known about how pre-service teachers’ prior knowledge shapes the quality of AI interaction, particularly through prompt engineering. Existing research frequently treats prompting as a procedural or syntactic task, neglecting its pedagogical and epistemic dimensions (ElSayary et al., 2025; Lee & Palmer, 2025). This creates a substantial gap in understanding how prompt formulation reflects deeper cognitive engagement and professional reasoning in educational contexts. Our study addresses this gap by offering a novel perspective, which is to prompt engineering to teachers’ AI-specific pedagogical and technological knowledge and skills. The latter is termed Intelligent-TPACK and AI literacy.

In accordance with this, an evaluation was conducted to ascertain how these knowledge domains inform the construction of adaptive, student-centered lesson plans with GenAI. The application of the KC framework to the analysis of prompt strategies 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 5.** Research model with standardized estimates.

demonstrates that prompts are not neutral inputs, but epistemic moves grounded in teachers’ instructional goals. The findings of our study provide empirical evidence that higher-phase prompts, reflecting negotiation and synthesis, contributed to the generation of more adaptive lesson plans. In turn, these higher-phase prompts are predicted by pre-service teachers’ AI-related knowledge. This study contributes to current debate by conceptualizing prompt engineering as a pedagogically grounded practice and emphasizing the necessity of integrating it into teacher education programs.

### _6.1._ _The features of prompting strategies and lesson plans_

The findings indicated that pre-service teachers frequently employed prompts at the negotiation of meaning (KCP3) level, sug- gesting a strong orientation towards pedagogical inquiry as opposed to mere information retrieval. This finding suggests that when confronted with a task necessitating adaptive design, many pre-service teachers instinctively endeavour to co-construct meaning with GenAI by posing clarifying questions, requesting elaborations, or seeking instructional alternatives.

It is noteworthy that prompts in the sharing information (KCP1) and discovery of dissonance (KCP2) stages were also common, reflecting early stages of interaction, where participants probed GenAI for foundational explanations or identified gaps in AI-generated content. However, the comparatively limited utilization of KCP4 (Modification of Synthesis) and KCP5 (Application) indicates a requirement for the scaffolding of pre-service teachers to facilitate deeper engagement in iterative and evaluative prompting. Prompt engineering has recently emerged as a widely discussed skill in both educational and professional contexts, especially with the increasing accessibility of GenAI tools like ChatGPT and Copilot. However, despite this growing interest, many end users, particularly novice educators, lack a conceptual understanding of what prompt engineering entails as a cognitive and pedagogical process (Knoth et al., 2024; Walter, 2024). This disconnection frequently leads to surface-level interactions with GenAI, where users focus on command syntax rather than strategic input formulation. In this regard, the KC framework offers a valuable lens for examining how novice users engage with GenAI. By situating prompts within progressive phases of epistemic engagement, the KC framework enables educators and researchers to evaluate the instructional quality embedded in prompt sequences (Gunawardena et al., 1997; Lucas et al., 2014).

Our study also demonstrates that the analysis of knowledge construction phases in the prompting can reveal not only the extent to which content is merely being retrieved, but also the presence of more sophisticated forms of pedagogical reasoning, such as the formulation of questions, the integration of ideas, and the refinement of concepts. In the present study, the KC framework was found to be particularly effective in differentiating between prompts that merely requested information and those that guided GenAI towards the co-construction of adaptive and meaningful learning experiences.

This has implications for pre-service teacher education. The development of prompt engineering competence should go beyond technical instruction. It is imperative that scaffolding strategies are incorporated to facilitate the progression of novice educators towards higher levels of knowledge construction in their interactions with AI.

Analysis of the lesson plans validated the connection between higher order prompting and adaptive teaching elements. The strongest lesson plans integrated multiple adaptive strategies, such as differentiated grouping, multimodal tools, and learner agency. For example, several plans asked students to choose among stations (drawing, experiments, storytelling), demonstrating both responsiveness to learner needs and AI-supported personalization. These features align with previous work emphasizing student- centered learning as a key outcome of effective GenAI integration (Cress & Kimmerle, 2023; Walter, 2024). While this study applied the KC framework to capture how pre-service teachers constructed their knowledge through human–AI interactions, future research could benefit from exploring alternative frameworks more directly rooted in knowledge building. For instance, Scardamalia and Bereiter’s Knowledge Building framework (2006) emphasizes collective advancement of ideas in a com- munity (Scardamalia and Bereiter, 2006), and Stahl’s (2000, 2017) work on collaborative knowledge building highlights group meaning making in online discourse. Such frameworks may provide complementary perspectives on how dialogic engagement with AI tools shapes not only individual pedagogical reasoning but also shared conceptual development. Incorporating these perspectives could further enrich understanding of how GenAI functions as a participant in knowledge-oriented discourse.

### _6.2._ _The role of pre-service teachers_′ _prior knowledge in generating adaptive lesson plan_

The findings further demonstrate significant associations between pre-service teachers’ Intelligent-TK, TPK, and AI literacy (awareness and usage) and their prompt engineering strategies. This finding aligns with earlier theoretical assumptions that the use of GenAI in teaching is not merely technical but also epistemic and pedagogical (Celik et al., 2022; Guggemos & Seufert, 2021). Spe- cifically, participants with higher Intelligent-TK and TPK scores were more likely to generate a greater number of prompts and engage in higher KC phases. Furthermore, these teachers were found to produce lesson plans with a greater number of adaptive features, including scaffolded learning sequences and increased student agency.

The structural model further suggested indirect effects, whereby TPK influenced lesson quality through the mediating role of prompting phases. This underscores the crucial function of pedagogical reasoning in the direction of GenAI outputs. In other words, the mere availability of AI tools is insufficient. It is imperative that educators possess the cognitive and pedagogical competencies to formulate prompts that guide AI in educationally meaningful directions.

It is interesting to note that general AI literacy (usage and awareness) supported prompt fluency, but that the ethical and evaluative aspects of AI literacy demonstrated weaker direct effects on prompting behaviour. This phenomenon may be attributable to the task’s emphasis on instructional design, as opposed to ethical decision-making. Nevertheless, ethical use of AI remains paramount, partic- ularly in the context of an escalating reliance on GenAI among educators (Holmes et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022).

The findings of this study demonstrate that prompting is not a neutral or mechanical act; rather, it is a pedagogically embedded process. Teachers who have a firm grasp on both the capabilities of AI and the instructional goals to be achieved are better positioned to co-construct effective and adaptive learning designs with GenAI. This finding lends support to the emerging calls for the integration of prompt engineering into teacher education curricula as a component of AI literacy and Intelligent-TPACK.

## 7. Conclusion

Pre-service teachers’ prompting with GenAI worked as an ongoing process shaped by what they already knew about teaching. Instead of using one-time commands, they adjusted their prompts based on the AI’s earlier answers. This shows that prompting is a thoughtful activity connected to planning and teaching goals. As their interaction with GenAI continued, their prompts became more focused and detailed. This pattern suggests that teachers were not just asking questions but building a kind of conversation with the tool to improve their lesson ideas.

The prompts provided by pre-service teachers using GenAI functioned as a continuous process, shaped by their previous teaching experiences. In lieu of utilizing one-time commands, a decision was made to adjust the prompts in accordance with the AI’s prior responses. This finding indicates that prompting is a deliberate activity associated with the formulation and execution of teaching objectives. As their interaction with GenAI continued, their prompts became more focused and detailed. This pattern suggests that teachers were not merely posing questions; rather, they were employing the tool to facilitate a form of dialogue, thereby enhancing their lesson plans.

Furthermore, the technological knowledge of pre-service teachers in artificial intelligence clearly affected the quality of their lesson plans. Those with stronger knowledge in using AI for teaching created prompts that led to more flexible, engaging, and personalized plans. Their effective use of GenAI shows their understanding of technology helps guide the tool in useful ways. Prompting became a way to apply their knowledge to practice. This underscores the significance of incorporating AI-related pedagogical competencies into teacher education curricula, thereby equipping future educators with the skills to utilize these tools in a meaningful and responsible manner.

## 8. Limitations and future research

Whilst the present study provides valuable insights into the prompt engineering strategies employed by pre-service teachers and the pedagogical use of GenAI tools, it is important to acknowledge the study’s limitations. Firstly, the sample consisted exclusively of Finnish pre-service teachers, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to other cultural or educational contexts. Future studies could expand the sample to include teachers from diverse educational systems to explore potential contextual differences in GenAI use.

Secondly, the study concentrated on a single instructional task (lesson planning), which may not encompass the entire spectrum of teaching practices or subject-specific prompt engineering strategies. It is recommended that future research endeavors involve the replication of this approach across a range of subjects, grade levels, and instructional goals. This would facilitate the development of a more comprehensive understanding of AI-assisted teaching design. This study utilized Microsoft Copilot as the GenAI tool for generating lesson plans. While the findings provide insight into how pre-service teachers engage in prompt engineering and knowledge construction with AI support, we acknowledge that outcomes may vary depending on the specific tool or version used. On the other hand, Copilot was a tool provided by the university that should be used as a first choice. The data was collected in a real pre-service teacher education context, which also contributes to this limitation. Different GenAI systems (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini) rely on distinct training data, model architecture, and interface designs, which can influence the style, quality, and adaptability of their outputs. As a result, teachers’ prompting strategies and the nature of the dialogic interaction may differ across tools. Future studies could compare multiple GenAI platforms to determine the extent to which observed patterns of knowledge construction reflect general features of human–AI collaboration versus characteristics unique to a given system.

Thirdly, although the AI literacy and Intelligent-TPACK scales have been validated and established, their use as self-report mea- sures may not fully reflect participants’ actual classroom practices. Future studies could combine observational or performance-based methods to enrich the findings.

Fourthly, the study excluded the final phase of the KC framework (agreement and application) since the implementation of the co- constructed lesson plan in real classroom settings is a prerequisite for this phase. While this decision was methodologically justified, it limits insight into how GenAI-supported planning translates into practical teaching actions. It is recommended that future research examine how AI-generated plans are enacted in real classrooms, with a view to capturing the full cycle of knowledge construction. Such research could be carried out, for example, in connection with teaching practice in schools.

Finally, although the KC framework has been found to be effective in categorizing the epistemic nature of prompts, there is a benefit to be gained from its utilization in conjunction with other frameworks (e.g., CoT, ToT) to capture strategic reasoning patterns in a more comprehensive manner. It is recommended that future research endeavors integrate multiple coding frameworks with a view to facilitating a more comprehensive understanding of the cognitive and metacognitive dimensions of prompt engineering. By addressing these limitations through further research, we can enhance our understanding of the meaningful integration of GenAI into teacher education and classroom practice.
